pitch: Exploit high-bandwidth RAM across many Cloudflare Edge Workers: explode a dataset too large for one machine into per-worker memory, run SIMD/MIMD-style anomaly detection and incremental training across workers, and persist only the deltas -- so a model can be trained on data that would not fit in one machine's memory. Target: live in 30 days.

nodes.title: Edge-RAM anomaly training pipeline
nodes.text:
Exploit high-bandwidth RAM across many Cloudflare Edge Workers: explode a dataset too large for one machine into per-worker memory, run SIMD/MIMD-style anomaly detection and incremental training across workers, and persist only the deltas -- so a model can be trained on data that would not fit in one machine's memory. Target: live in 30 days.
Listed child items: Platform feasibility spike, Ingest and sharding, In-memory compute kernel, Cross-worker orchestration and delta exchange, Incremental training and persistence.
nodes.covers_why: Root node; no single 'covers' judgement applies to the whole pitch.

nodes.title: Platform feasibility spike
nodes.text:
Before building anything else: confirm whether Cloudflare Workers actually provide the memory-bandwidth and cross-worker memory-sharing primitives this architecture assumes.
Listed child items: Per-isolate memory ceiling, Shared or pooled memory across workers, WASM SIMD availability.
nodes.covers_why: Memory ceiling, shared memory, and SIMD availability are the three concrete platform facts the rest of the architecture depends on; nothing else about platform feasibility is being assumed here.

nodes.title: Per-isolate memory ceiling
nodes.text:
Confirm the actual memory limit one Cloudflare Worker isolate gets today, and whether any Cloudflare product or plan tier offers more, since every downstream chunk size depends on this number.
Listed child items: Week-1 spike: allocate-until-killed test.
nodes.why: Documented, but the exact current figure needs checking against live docs and this account's plan before anything is sized against it.
nodes.covers_why: The one child (the spike) is the entire resolution path for this question.

nodes.title: Week-1 spike: allocate-until-killed test
nodes.text: Deploy a Worker that allocates memory until the platform kills it, on this account's actual plan tier, and record the real ceiling.
nodes.why: Cheapest possible way to replace a documentation guess with a measured number; half a day of work, gates every sizing decision after it.

nodes.title: Shared or pooled memory across workers
nodes.text:
Confirm whether two Cloudflare Worker isolates can read or write the same physical memory directly, at anything close to local RAM bandwidth -- or whether all cross-worker data movement necessarily goes over the network.
Listed child items: Week-1 spike: cross-worker transfer benchmark.
nodes.why: My own read: Workers isolates are deliberately memory-isolated for security; there is no documented shared-memory fabric between them, so 'RAM speed across edge workers' as literally pitched is very likely not a real primitive. That belief could be wrong or stale, and it is the single highest-consequence assumption in the whole pitch, so it gets a live spike rather than being asserted as fact.
nodes.covers_why: The one child (the spike) is the entire resolution path for this question.

nodes.title: Week-1 spike: cross-worker transfer benchmark
nodes.text: Try to move a block of data from one Worker invocation to another without going through a network-facing API, and measure whatever bandwidth is actually achieved.
nodes.why: If this comes back at network speed, not RAM speed, the architecture needs reframing now -- as sharded compute with network-exchanged deltas, not shared memory -- before 29 more days are spent building on the wrong assumption.

nodes.title: WASM SIMD availability
nodes.text: Confirm the Workers runtime's WebAssembly engine supports the SIMD instruction proposal, and get a rough sense of the realistic speedup for a numeric anomaly-detection kernel.
nodes.why: This part of the pitch is real and shipped (V8's WASM SIMD proposal); lower stakes, and answerable by reading current docs rather than a live spike.

nodes.title: Ingest and sharding
nodes.text:
Split the source dataset into per-worker chunks that fit inside whatever the real memory ceiling turns out to be, and dispatch them to many workers in parallel.
Listed child items: Chunk sizing against the memory ceiling, Where the source dataset lives, Worker fan-out limits.
nodes.covers_why: Chunk sizing, source location, and fan-out limits are the three questions that fully determine how data gets from source to worker.

nodes.title: Chunk sizing against the memory ceiling
nodes.text: Decide chunk size once the real per-isolate memory ceiling is known, leaving headroom for the running process, not just the raw data.
nodes.why: A direct decision, but it cannot be made responsibly until feas-mem's real number exists.

nodes.title: Where the source dataset lives
nodes.text: Choose where the large source dataset is actually read from -- Cloudflare R2, an external object store, or a streamed feed -- and how far a Worker can read into it per invocation.
nodes.why: An architecture choice with real cost implications (R2 has no egress fee to Workers, external storage may), not something the plan itself has data to force.

nodes.title: Worker fan-out limits
nodes.text: Confirm how many Workers a single request can realistically fan out to in parallel, given Cloudflare's subrequest and concurrency limits on this account's plan.
nodes.why: Documented but plan-tier-dependent; determines whether 'many workers in parallel' means dozens or thousands for this account.

nodes.title: In-memory compute kernel
nodes.text:
Run a vectorised (SIMD) anomaly-detection pass over each worker's own chunk, inside that worker's own memory, within the platform's per-invocation time budget.
Listed child items: Pick a streaming-friendly anomaly algorithm, Per-invocation compute budget, Implement and benchmark the SIMD kernel.
nodes.covers_why: Algorithm choice, time budget, and implementation cover picking, sizing, and building the kernel.

nodes.title: Pick a streaming-friendly anomaly algorithm
nodes.text: Choose an anomaly-detection method that can run one chunk at a time with no view of the whole dataset (online/incremental), since no single worker ever sees more than its own shard.
nodes.why: A real design choice (e.g. streaming z-score/IQR variants, an online isolation-forest variant, or a sketch-based method) with accuracy trade-offs the plan alone can't resolve.

nodes.title: Per-invocation compute budget
nodes.text:
Measure the real CPU and wall-clock time one Worker invocation gets, and compare it against how much computation the chosen kernel actually needs per chunk.
Listed child items: Week-1 spike: representative workload timing.
nodes.why: Workers have a hard per-invocation time limit; 'run all my high computation' inside one invocation is only true if the chunk's workload actually fits that limit, which has not been measured.
nodes.covers_why: The one child (the spike) is the entire resolution path for this question.

nodes.title: Week-1 spike: representative workload timing
nodes.text: Run a realistic chunk of the actual computation inside a real Worker invocation and measure wall-clock time against the platform's per-invocation limit.
nodes.why: If a chunk's workload doesn't fit one invocation, the plan needs smaller chunks or a multi-invocation pattern per chunk -- worth knowing in week 1, not week 3.

nodes.title: Implement and benchmark the SIMD kernel
nodes.text: Build the chosen anomaly-detection kernel in WASM with SIMD, and benchmark it against a plain (non-SIMD) version to confirm the speedup is real for this workload.
nodes.why: Real implementation work; only worth doing once the algorithm choice and the time-budget spike both say this is viable, so it is not a week-1 item.

nodes.title: Cross-worker orchestration and delta exchange
nodes.text:
Coordinate many independent Workers -- each running the same kernel on different data, the MIMD part of the pitch -- and move only the anomalous deltas between them, since there is no shared memory to pass full results through.
Listed child items: Choose the coordination primitive, Define the delta format, Define the reduce step.
nodes.covers_why: The three children cover choosing the mechanism and the data format, but not failure handling -- what happens when a worker crashes mid-computation, or a delta is lost -- which any real coordination layer needs and none of the three children address.

nodes.title: Choose the coordination primitive
nodes.text: Pick how workers get coordinated and how work gets handed out: Durable Objects for stateful coordination, Queues for work distribution, or an external orchestrator outside Cloudflare.
nodes.why: A real architecture decision with cost and latency trade-offs the plan can't make unilaterally.

nodes.title: Define the delta format
nodes.text: Define what each worker actually emits when it finds an anomaly -- small enough to move cheaply over the network, since that is now the only channel between workers.
nodes.why: Depends on both the coordination primitive and on feas-shared's real answer about what channel exists at all.

nodes.title: Define the reduce step
nodes.text: Define how deltas from many independent workers get merged into one picture -- deduplicated, ordered, or aggregated as appropriate.
nodes.why: A design detail that follows once the coordination primitive is chosen; not needed to de-risk the plan in week 1.

nodes.title: Incremental training and persistence
nodes.text:
Accumulate a trained model from a stream of deltas arriving from many short-lived invocations, and persist the running state somewhere that survives between them.
Listed child items: Where the accumulating state lives, Confirm the model type supports incremental updates.
nodes.covers_why: Where state lives and whether the model supports incremental updates are the two questions that determine whether 'train across many short-lived invocations' is coherent at all.

nodes.title: Where the accumulating state lives
nodes.text: Decide where the running model state is persisted between invocations, since Workers themselves are stateless and short-lived: Durable Objects, KV, R2, or an external database.
nodes.why: A real, consequential choice (Durable Objects give strong consistency but add latency; KV/R2 are eventually consistent and cheaper) the plan can't make alone.

nodes.title: Confirm the model type supports incremental updates
nodes.text: Confirm the chosen model type can actually be updated incrementally from a stream of deltas, since a full retrain on every delta will not fit the time or memory budget.
nodes.why: Depends on kernel-algo's choice; some anomaly-detection methods have well-known online variants, others don't, and that isn't knowable until the algorithm is picked.
